children: Federal aviation officials are preparing to launch an AI-powered air-traffic tool in one of the nation's busiest corridors as soon as Monday.

The software, known as Smart, is expected to help the Federal Aviation Administration and airlines reduce delays and cancellations and find routes for flights when disruptions scramble air traffic. It will first debut in the Washington, D.C., area ahead of a broader nationwide rollout, according to government and industry officials.

Smart stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. The software has the ability to analyze airline schedules and factors such as weather, airport runway capacity and operational constraints to predict air-traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur.

When fully rolled out across U.S. airspace, the software is supposed to act as something like the brains of the nation's air-traffic control system. The firm Air Space Intelligence won a $875 million, 12-year government contract earlier this year to build out Smart and a related system.

The Trump administration has directed billions of dollars of spending to upgrade the nation's aging air-traffic infrastructure with new technology. The administration has also been trying to ramp up hiring and training of air-traffic controllers. Staffing shortages at air-traffic facilities are frequent sources of disruptions.

FAA officials have been discussing with airlines how to coordinate their schedules as part of the software's broader rollout. Industry officials have had questions about how the system would work, particularly given carriers' fierce competition to operate flights at certain times of day.

"The way we manage traffic today is chaotic, and we can do better," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, a former regional airline executive, said during Senate testimony earlier this year. "We need to manage that at the FAA, rather than rely on commercial airlines to simply schedule however they want."
The tool's initial rollout is on a smaller scale than some aviation industry officials had anticipated after months of planning.

Government officials said Smart's debut was always planned to be limited before validating the software and expanding its capabilities, such as spacing out arrival times and planning routes days in advance. For now, it will be used as a decision-making aid when problems arise.
Federal officials are also planning to unveil a central office for the tool at the Transportation Department's headquarters on Monday, according to government and industry officials.

Airlines for America, an industry trade group, said the Smart tool has the potential to bolster safety, increase capacity and improve efficiency that will benefit travelers and shippers. The group, which represents major U.S. carriers, called it "one of the most exciting and bold initiatives taken on by the FAA in decades."
